questions.prompt: A hospital manager writes: "Are our clinics doing well on waiting?" The appointments table has one row per appointment, with clinic, booking date, visit date and minutes waited. Which rewrite is ready for an analysis plan?
options: Which of our clinics are performing badly on waiting, and which well?
Why do some clinics make their patients wait longer than others?
How long do patients wait at our clinics before they are seen?
What is the median wait per appointment, by clinic, in 2025?
questions.explanation: It names the unit (an appointment), the variable (minutes waited), the comparison (by clinic) and the period.
misconceptions: Keeps a judgement word, "badly", that has no measure
Asks for a cause, which a table of appointments cannot give
Names a variable and no comparison or unit

questions.prompt: A library has a loans table (one row per loan) and a members table (one row per member). An analyst counts the rows of the loans table for 2025 and reports "18,400 people borrowed a book". What is wrong?
options: A count cannot be reported without a percentage beside it
The loans table should have been joined to the members table before counting
The count is of loans, so a member with ten loans is counted ten times
The year 2025 is too short a period for a count of members
questions.explanation: One row is one loan. Counting rows counts loans; people need a count of distinct members.
misconceptions: Confuses a presentation habit with the error, which is the unit
Believes a join fixes the unit; a join alone still leaves one row per loan
Looks for the fault in the period, not in what a row is

questions.prompt: A plan entry reads: question "How do complaints differ across branches?", table "complaints", unit "one complaint", variables ["branch"], comparison "look at complaints by branch". Which part fails a plan checklist first?
options: The unit, because a single complaint is too small a unit to analyse on its own
The comparison, because it does not say what is set against what
The question, because it does not end with the name of the branch concerned
The table, because complaints need a second table before they can be counted
questions.explanation: A comparison names the two things compared and the measure; "look at" names neither, and a rate needs its denominator.
misconceptions: Mistakes a fine-grained unit for a fault; the unit is correct for this table
Invents a rule about the wording of the question
Counting complaints needs one table; it is the rate that needs a second

questions.prompt: An analyst tabulates average basket value by weekday, by store and by payment method, and notices that card payments on Thursdays are highest. She reports: "Thursday card payments are the most valuable". How should the finding be labelled?
options: Confirmed, because it was computed from the complete sales table of the year
Confirmed, because a difference this large between groups cannot be chance
Exploratory, because sales data can never be used to confirm any pattern
Exploratory, because the comparison was chosen after looking at many cuts
questions.explanation: The pattern was picked because it stood out among many comparisons; the data that suggested it cannot also confirm it.
misconceptions: Believes complete data makes a searched pattern confirmed
Takes the size of a gap as proof that it was not selected
Thinks the kind of data decides; it is the order of question and look that decides

questions.prompt: A pattern was found by exploring the 2024 survey: members rate evening classes higher. What would make it a confirmed finding?
options: Writing it down now and testing it on the 2025 survey, not yet looked at
Recomputing it on the 2024 survey with a different software package and seed
Finding a second pattern in the 2024 survey that points the same way as this
Showing the 2024 chart to three colleagues who all agree with the reading
questions.explanation: A fresh test fixes the comparison first and uses data that played no part in finding the pattern.
misconceptions: Confuses reproducing a number with testing a claim
More searching in the same data adds comparisons, not evidence
Agreement about a chart is not a test of what the chart suggests

questions.prompt: An orders table should have one row per order. It has 52,300 rows and 52,000 distinct order numbers. The 300 repeated order numbers each appear twice, with different delivery dates. What goes into the issue log?
options: Record 300 orders with conflicting rows and ask the owner which is right
Keep the row with the later delivery date, which is the more recent one
Drop the second row of each pair, since they are plainly double entries
Average the two delivery dates of each pair and keep one row per order
questions.explanation: Rows that share a key and differ are a conflict, not a copy; choosing between them is the owner's decision.
misconceptions: Invents a rule that the later row is right
Treats conflicting rows as exact copies
Creates a delivery date that never existed

questions.prompt: In a customer survey, income is missing for 7% of respondents overall: 3% of those under 40 and 19% of those over 60. An analyst reports mean income from the rows that have a value. What is the main risk?
options: The mean rests on 7% fewer rows, so its standard error is slightly larger
The 7% is too small a share to affect any summary
The mean cannot be computed while any value is missing
The mean describes younger respondents more than all respondents
questions.explanation: The missing values sit with one group, so the rows that remain over-represent the other.
misconceptions: Sees only the loss of rows, not who is lost
Judges by the overall share and ignores where the missing values are
Confuses a software default with a statistical problem

questions.prompt: A column "age" in a membership table has a minimum of 0, a maximum of 120 and a spike of 412 rows at exactly 0. The form allows the field to be skipped. What is the most likely reading, and the first step?
options: 0 stands for "not given"; set those values to missing and record 412 rows
The spike is random noise in a large table; smooth it away with a wider bin
412 members are infants enrolled by their parents; keep the values as they are
0 is a data-entry error for 10; add ten years to those rows and record it
questions.explanation: A spike at a default value in an optional field is a code for missing, not a measurement.
misconceptions: Treats a structural spike as sampling noise
Takes a default value for a real age
Replaces one invented value with another

questions.prompt: Delivery times at a courier have a median of 2 days for city A and for city B, and the same quartiles. In city A nearly all parcels take 1 to 3 days. In city B half take 1 day and half take 3 to 4 days. Which chart shows the difference?
options: A box plot of delivery days for each city
A pie chart of the share of parcels delivered in each city
A bar chart of the median number of delivery days for each city
A histogram of delivery days for each city, one bin per day
questions.explanation: Two humps and one hump can share the same five numbers; only the histogram shows the shape.
misconceptions: A box draws the five numbers, which are equal here
Shows the size of each city, not the delivery times
A single number per city, and the numbers are equal

questions.prompt: A gym chain compares the visit lengths of 9,000 standard members and 600 premium members with two histograms on the same count axis. The premium histogram is a flat strip along the bottom. What is the repair?
options: Replace both histograms with the two group means
Remove the standard members so that the premium members can be seen
Give each histogram its own count axis and place them side by side
Draw each group as shares of its own total, on a common share axis
questions.explanation: Shares put groups of unequal size on the same footing, so the shapes can be compared.
misconceptions: Throws away the shapes that the question is about
Removes the comparison the chart was drawn for
Makes the shapes visible but invites comparing bar heights across different scales

questions.prompt: House prices in a district have a mean of 1.9 million riyals and a median of 1.2 million. A report says "the typical house costs 1.9 million". What should it say?
options: No typical price can be given for a skewed variable
The typical house costs 1.2 million; a few very expensive houses pull the mean up
The typical house costs 1.9 million; the mean uses every house and is more accurate
The typical house costs 1.55 million, the midpoint of mean and median
questions.explanation: Half of the houses cost less than the median; with a long right tail most houses cost less than the mean.
misconceptions: Gives up where the median does the job
Takes "uses every value" for "describes a typical value"
Averages two summaries that answer different questions

questions.prompt: Two branches both have a mean rating of 3.5 on a 1 to 5 scale. In branch A nearly everyone gives 3 or 4. In branch B half give 5 and half give 2. Which report lets a manager see the difference?
options: The mean rating of each branch, given with two decimals
The median rating of each branch
The total number of ratings of each branch
The share of customers at each score, for each branch
questions.explanation: Shares by score show that branch B has a large dissatisfied group that an average conceals.
misconceptions: More decimals of the same number show nothing new
One number per branch again; it cannot show a split
Shows how many answered, not what they answered

questions.prompt: A caption reads: "Median spend per visitor: 310 riyals." The table behind it has 8,000 visitors, of whom 2,100 gave no spend; most of those were visitors on free school trips. What is missing from the caption?
options: The number of visitors the median rests on and who was left out
The mean spend as well, so that the reader has both summaries at hand
The standard deviation of spend
The date on which the table was exported
questions.explanation: A summary carries its number of values and what was excluded; here a quarter of the visitors, of one kind, are not in it.
misconceptions: A second summary of the same rows does not reveal the excluded rows
Describes spread among the included rows only
Useful for the record, and it does not tell the reader who is missing

questions.prompt: An analyst joins a table of 9,000 orders to a table of 30 warehouses to add each warehouse's region. The result has 9,640 rows. What should the analyst conclude first?
options: The join added the 640 orders that had been missing before
Some orders were placed twice and the join has revealed them
Some warehouse appears more than once in the warehouse table
A join always adds a few rows, so the result can be used as it is
questions.explanation: A join to a table with one row per warehouse cannot add rows. More rows than before means a key is repeated on the other side.
misconceptions: Reads extra rows as recovered data; a join cannot create orders
Looks for the fault in the orders, which the join did not change
Treats a changed row count as normal and skips the cheapest check there is

questions.prompt: Across 200 shops on 365 days, daily footfall and daily sales correlate at 0.35. Summed over all shops by week, the two series correlate at 0.80. Which sentence is correct?
options: The weekly figure is the true correlation and the daily one is wrong
The daily figure is the true correlation, since it uses more rows
Both are correct, each for its own unit, and a report names the unit
The two figures disagree, so one of the two tables has an error
questions.explanation: Adding up shops and days averages away what is particular to one shop on one day. A correlation belongs to the table it was computed on.
misconceptions: Believes aggregation reveals a truer value; it answers a different question
Believes more rows make a coefficient more correct
Expects one coefficient per pair of variables whatever the unit

questions.prompt: A scatter plot of 300,000 deliveries (distance against delivery time) is a solid block. The operations manager asks: "How much longer does a delivery take at 20 km than at 5 km?" Which display answers that?
options: The same scatter plot drawn with smaller and fainter points
A heatmap of the number of deliveries by distance and time
The correlation coefficient of distance and delivery time
The median delivery time inside bands of distance
questions.explanation: A "how much" question about y at given x is answered by a summary of y inside bins of x.
misconceptions: Transparency shows where points are dense, not a value of y at a given x
A heatmap shows where deliveries are, and leaves the reader to guess the middle
One coefficient says how closely points follow a line, not how many minutes

questions.prompt: A ministry lists the five schools with the most pupils absent last week. All five are among the largest schools in the country. What does the list show?
options: Mainly which schools are the largest
Which schools have an absence problem
That large schools cause more absence
That absence was recorded wrongly
questions.explanation: A count of absent pupils follows the number of pupils. Without a rate the list ranks schools by size.
misconceptions: Reads a count as a rate
Reads a pattern produced by size as an effect of size
Suspects the recording when the measure is the issue

questions.prompt: A bank wants to know at which branch a customer visit most often ends in a complaint. It has complaints per branch, customer visits per branch, staff per branch and accounts per branch. Which rate answers the question?
options: Complaints per thousand accounts held at the branch
Complaints per thousand customer visits to the branch
Complaints per member of staff at the branch
Complaints at the branch as a share of all complaints
questions.explanation: The denominator is whoever could have produced the event: here, a customer visit.
misconceptions: Counts accounts, many of which never visit a branch
Measures workload per employee, which is a different question
A share of all complaints is the count again, divided by a constant

questions.prompt: A table of complaint rates by clinic and age group shows the highest rate, 40 per thousand, for one clinic's patients over 80: 2 complaints from 50 visits. The publication rule asks for at least 10 complaints and 1,000 visits. What does the analyst do?
options: Withhold the cell and mark it as withheld in the table
Publish the 2 complaints but not the 50 visits
Replace the cell with the clinic's rate for all ages
Publish it with a note that the rate is the highest
questions.explanation: Two complaints give a rate that one more complaint would move by half, and they may identify the two patients. The cell is held back and marked.
misconceptions: Publishes the part that could identify people and hides the denominator
Puts a different number in the cell without saying so
Highlights exactly the number that rests on the fewest cases

questions.prompt: A shop ran a sale in June 2024 and again in June 2025. June 2025 sales were 3% above June 2024, in line with the usual yearly growth. A manager says the 2025 sale had no effect. What is wrong with that?
options: Nothing: growth of 3% is what a month without a sale shows
The comparison month also had a sale, so the effect cancels
June should have been compared with May of the same year
A single month is too short to compute any growth figure
questions.explanation: A change on a year earlier measures the difference between two years. An event present in both disappears from it.
misconceptions: Forgets that the reference month was itself a sale month
Compares with the month before, which mixes the sale with the season
Rejects the comparison for its length when its reference is the issue

questions.prompt: Visits to a park were 20,000 in April 2024, a month without events. Visits usually grow 5% a year. A festival took place in April 2025 and visits were 26,250. By how much did April 2025 exceed its baseline?
options: By 5%, the usual growth from one year to the next
By 20%, since 5,250 extra visits is a fifth of 26,250
By 25%, since the baseline for April 2025 is 21,000
By 31%, since 26,250 is 31% more than 20,000
questions.explanation: The baseline is the same month a year earlier grown by the usual 5%: 21,000. And 26,250 divided by 21,000 is 1.25.
misconceptions: Gives the trend, not the excess over it
Divides the excess by the actual value, not by the baseline
Credits the festival with the usual yearly growth as well

questions.prompt: A monthly series of electricity use shows a peak every August, each a little higher than the last, and one tall spike in a February. Which reading names the three parts correctly?
options: The August peaks are events, the rise is the season, the spike is the trend
The August peaks are the trend, the rise is an event, the spike is the season
The August peaks are the season, the rise is the trend, the spike is an event
All three are the season, since each one recurs or could recur
questions.explanation: What repeats at the same time each year is the season, the slow change of level is the trend, and what stands outside both is an event.
misconceptions: Calls a yearly repeat an event
Calls a yearly repeat a trend
Folds everything into the season and loses the question

questions.prompt: A hospital's average length of stay rose from 4.0 to 4.6 days in a year. In both of its wards, surgical and medical, the average stay fell. How can both be true?
options: A larger share of patients was in the ward with longer stays
Average stays cannot be compared between two different years
The hospital average is the plain mean of the two ward averages
One of the two ward averages must have been miscalculated
questions.explanation: The hospital average is a weighted average of the wards. It can rise while both ward averages fall if the mix moves to the ward with longer stays.
misconceptions: Gives up the comparison; it only needs the mix to be stated
Forgets the weights: a plain mean of two falling numbers would fall
Assumes an arithmetic error where there is a change of weights

questions.prompt: In 2024 a service had 80% routine cases (score 4.5) and 20% complex cases (score 3.5). In 2025 the scores were 4.6 and 3.6, and the mix was 50% routine, 50% complex. What was the 2025 score at the 2024 mix?
options: 4.10, the average of 4.6 and 3.6 with equal weights
4.30, the score of 2024 carried over unchanged
4.40, from 0.8 times 4.6 plus 0.2 times 3.6
4.60, the score of the larger group in 2024
questions.explanation: Hold the weights at 80% and 20% and use the 2025 scores: 3.68 + 0.72 = 4.40, up from 4.30, while the score as surveyed fell to 4.10.
misconceptions: Uses the 2025 mix, which gives the figure as surveyed
Uses the 2024 scores as well as the 2024 mix
Takes one group for the whole

questions.prompt: A regional director sees that the overall pass rate fell while it rose in every course type, because more people now take the harder courses. She asks which number to put in the annual report. What is the best advice?
options: Only the overall rate, since it is the official figure
Neither, since the two results contradict each other
Only the rates by course type, since the overall rate misleads
The overall rate, the rates by type and the change of mix, together
questions.explanation: Each figure answers a different question. Printed together with the change of mix, they explain each other.
misconceptions: Leaves the reader to conclude that teaching got worse
Treats two correct tables as an error
Hides a true and relevant fact about the average learner

questions.prompt: A chart shows one circle per city: population on x, average rent on y, and the circle's colour gives the region. In the terms of a grammar of graphics, what is "region to colour"?
options: The colour scale
An encoding
The mark used
A facet variable
questions.explanation: An encoding maps a column to a visual channel. The mark is the circle; the scale decides which colour each region gets.
misconceptions: The scale turns values into colours once the mapping exists
The mark is the shape drawn for each row, here a circle
A facet would split the regions into separate panels

questions.prompt: A report must let readers compare the budgets of 15 departments as precisely as possible. Which encoding of the budget serves that best?
options: The area of a circle for each department
The depth of colour of a tile for each department
The position of a point or the end of a bar on one axis
The angle of a slice in a pie chart of all departments
questions.explanation: Position on a common scale is read most precisely. Area, angle and colour intensity are read with much larger errors.
misconceptions: Area is read imprecisely; a reader underestimates large circles
Colour intensity is the least precise channel for a quantity
Fifteen angles cannot be ranked by eye

questions.prompt: An analyst draws average exam scores of 6 schools, between 71 and 78, as points on an axis from 70 to 80. A reviewer says: "The axis must start at zero." Who is right?
options: The reviewer: every chart of quantities needs a zero baseline
The reviewer: without zero the differences are exaggerated
The analyst, provided the chart states the range of its axis
The analyst: axis ranges are a matter of taste, not accuracy
questions.explanation: A point is read by its position, not by a length from a base. Its axis may start where the data starts, if the chart says so. Bars would need zero.
misconceptions: Applies the rule for bars and areas to every mark
True for a bar, whose length is read; not for a point
Right answer for the wrong reason: for bars the range is a matter of accuracy

questions.prompt: Monthly sales of 6 regions are drawn as small multiples. The reader has to see which region sells the most. Which scales fit?
options: A separate y scale fitted to each panel
One shared y scale for all six panels
A separate y scale from zero for each panel
A shared x scale and no y axis at all
questions.explanation: Comparing levels across panels needs heights that mean the same thing in every panel: a shared scale.
misconceptions: Makes every region fill its panel, so all six look the same size
Keeps proportions inside a panel and still hides which region is largest
Removes the only means of reading a level

questions.prompt: A chart with a separate y scale for each of its panels carries no note about the scales. What is the most likely misreading?
options: Readers will think the panels show different variables
Readers will be unable to see the shape of each series
Readers will compare heights across panels as if on one scale
Readers will assume that the time axes differ between panels
questions.explanation: People compare heights across panels by default. With free scales that comparison is false, so the chart has to say that scales differ.
misconceptions: The panels are labelled; the variable is not in doubt
Free scales are what makes each shape visible
Nothing suggests different time axes; the y scale is what changed

questions.prompt: A bar chart shows customer satisfaction of 88% last year and 91% this year on a y axis from 85% to 92%. This year's bar is twice as tall as last year's. What is the fault and the repair?
options: A picked window; show more years on the same axis
A count for a rate; divide by the number of customers
A cut baseline; start the bars at zero or use points
Two axes; plot each year in a panel of its own
questions.explanation: A bar is read by its length. On an axis from 85 the lengths show 3 and 6, not 88 and 91.
misconceptions: More years would help context and leave the bars as misleading as before
The value is already a rate
There is one axis and one series

questions.prompt: A slide plots advertising spend on the left axis and sales on the right axis over 24 months. The two lines overlap almost perfectly, and the title says "Sales follow advertising". Why is this weak evidence?
options: The author chose both axis ranges, and so chose the overlap
Lines are the wrong mark for monthly data of this kind
Two variables may never be shown on the same chart
Sales and spend are in different currencies or units
questions.explanation: With two free axes, any two series can be made to overlap. A scatter of one against the other shows the relation at its true strength.
misconceptions: A line suits a monthly series; the mark is not the issue
Too strong: a scatter plot shows two variables on one chart, honestly
Different units are the reason for two axes, not the reason the overlap misleads

questions.prompt: A headline reads "Road accidents down 30%". The chart beside it compares last August with this August. Five years of monthly data exist, and last August included a week of floods. Which fault is this?
options: A picked window
A running total
Uneven steps
A cut baseline
questions.explanation: Two months were chosen out of sixty, one of them unusual. The repair is the whole series with the flood month named.
misconceptions: Nothing is cumulated here
Both periods are one month long
Nothing is said about where the axis starts

questions.prompt: After repairing a misleading chart, an analyst wants to know whether the repair mattered. Which test tells her?
options: Whether the numbers in the two charts are exactly the same
Whether the repaired chart looks more professional than the original
Whether the repaired chart uses fewer colours and less ink
Whether a reader would conclude something different from the two charts
questions.explanation: A fault matters when the published chart makes a reader believe something the data does not say. Write both conclusions and compare them.
misconceptions: The numbers are usually the same; the impression is what changed
Polish is not the measure of honesty
Economy of ink is a style rule, not a test of what is concluded

questions.prompt: A map-like grid shows the complaint rate of 40 districts, from low to high. Which kind of palette fits?
options: Forty distinct hues, one for each district
A rainbow from red through green to violet
Two hues, red for bad and green for good
One hue running from light to dark
questions.explanation: A quantity from low to high takes a sequential palette: one hue, light to dark.
misconceptions: Hues tell names apart and cannot order a quantity
A rainbow shows bands where the data has none
Two hues suit a quantity with a midpoint, and red against green fails many readers

questions.prompt: A line chart with five coloured lines will be printed in a black-and-white bulletin. Which change keeps every line identifiable?
options: Use five darker colours with higher contrast
Move the legend from the right to the bottom
Label each line at its end and vary the dash pattern
Make all five lines the same thickness
questions.explanation: Direct labels and a second channel carry the identity without colour.
misconceptions: Darker colours become similar greys in print
A legend keyed by colour is useless in grey, wherever it sits
Equal thickness removes a possible cue and adds none

questions.prompt: A team produces every chart in Arabic and in English by copying the English notebook and translating the labels by hand. Three months later the two versions of one chart show different numbers. What would have prevented it?
options: A second analyst who checks each translated chart before it is released
Arabic labels written directly into the data in place of the English ones
One function that draws the chart, with the texts read from a label file
An image editor used to replace the texts on the exported English chart
questions.explanation: With one function and one data path, the two versions can differ only in their words.
misconceptions: Review finds some differences after the fact; it does not remove their cause
Translating the data breaks every join and filter that uses the original values
Editing an image cuts the chart off from its data altogether

questions.prompt: An analyst has delivery times for two courier firms and wants to know whether the difference of 0.4 day between their means could arise if the firm made no difference. Which procedure fits?
options: Repeat the calculation with a different random seed
Resample the deliveries of each firm with replacement
Sort the deliveries and compare the two medians
Shuffle the firm labels and recompute the difference
questions.explanation: Shuffling the labels creates the situation in which the firm makes no difference; the p-value is the share of shuffles with a gap as large as the observed one.
misconceptions: A seed changes the draws of a procedure; it is not a procedure
Gives an interval for each mean, not a test of "no difference"
Changes the summary and gives no measure of chance

questions.prompt: A permutation test of a training programme's effect on sales gives p = 0.40 with 30 salespeople in each group. Which sentence may go in the report?
options: This data shows no clear effect of the training
The training has a 40% chance of working
The training has a 60% chance of working
The training has no effect on sales
questions.explanation: A large p-value is an absence of evidence for an effect in this data. With 30 per group, a useful effect could easily go unseen.
misconceptions: Reads the p-value as the probability of the hypothesis
Reads one minus the p-value as the probability of the hypothesis
Reads absence of evidence as evidence of absence

questions.prompt: Sensor readings are taken every minute from 12 machines for a week. An analyst bootstraps the 120,000 readings to get an interval for the mean temperature and finds it extremely narrow. Why should it not be trusted?
options: A week of readings is too short a period for any bootstrap to work
The bootstrap is valid only for normally distributed readings
An interval can never be computed for a mean of sensor readings
Readings of one machine are alike; the 12 machines are the units
questions.explanation: There are 12 independent units, not 120,000. Resampling readings as if independent makes the interval far too narrow.
misconceptions: The length of the period is not what breaks the independence
The bootstrap does not assume a normal distribution
Too strong: the interval is fine once the right unit is resampled

questions.prompt: A league table ranks 50 branches by mean customer rating. The top three and the bottom three are all among the smallest branches. What is the most likely reason?
options: Small branches give either very good or very bad service
Means of small groups vary more, so they reach both ends
Customers of small branches rate more carelessly
The ranking was computed with the wrong formula
questions.explanation: The fewer the ratings, the more a mean moves by chance. Extremes of a ranking collect small groups for that reason alone.
misconceptions: Explains by quality what sampling variation already explains
Invents a behaviour for which there is no evidence
The formula is right; the missing piece is the uncertainty

questions.prompt: Two teams have mean resolution times with 95% intervals of 30 to 38 hours and 35 to 45 hours. An analyst must say whether the teams differ. What is the right next step?
options: Compute an interval for the difference between the two means
State that they are equal, since the intervals overlap
State that they differ, since the means are different
Widen both intervals to 99% and compare them again
questions.explanation: Overlap leaves the question open. The interval of the difference answers it directly.
misconceptions: Overlap does not prove equality
Ignores the uncertainty of both means
Wider intervals overlap more and still do not address the difference

questions.prompt: A chart shows mean satisfaction by service channel with 95% bootstrap intervals. Which sentence belongs in its caption?
options: The intervals show that the survey is free of any bias
The intervals cover sampling variation, not who chose to answer
The intervals prove which channel customers really prefer
The intervals contain 95% of all the customers' ratings
questions.explanation: An interval covers the variation from drawing another sample. It says nothing about non-response or the wording of the question.
misconceptions: An interval cannot detect or remove bias
An interval supports a comparison; it does not prove a preference
Confuses an interval for a mean with the spread of the ratings

questions.prompt: An analyst tests 20 unrelated survey questions for a difference between two regions, each at the 0.05 level. In truth there is no difference on any of them. About how likely is at least one "significant" result?
options: About 5%
About 20%
About 64%
About 95%
questions.explanation: One minus 0.95 to the power 20 is 0.64. With many comparisons, a chance finding is the likely outcome.
misconceptions: The level of a single test, not of twenty
Guesses a figure near the number of tests
Confuses the chance of a false alarm with the confidence level

questions.prompt: Which of these findings is confirmed, in the sense used in this course?
options: The strongest of 30 correlations found in last year's sales data
A result that three analysts each found plausible on inspection
A pattern seen in January and seen again by rereading January's data
A difference stated in the March plan and tested once on April's data
questions.explanation: What confirms a finding is the order of events: the question is written down before the data that answers it is looked at.
misconceptions: Chosen after looking, from many comparisons
Agreement among readers is not a test
The same data cannot suggest a pattern and confirm it

questions.prompt: While exploring, an analyst notices that customers who call on Mondays cancel more often. The pattern was one of many she looked at. What should her report say?
options: "Monday callers cancel more often (p = 0.03)", as a finding
"Exploratory: one of many cuts; to be tested on next quarter's calls"
Nothing: exploratory patterns do not belong in a report
"Monday calls cause cancellations; move staff to Mondays"
questions.explanation: An exploratory pattern is reported with its label, the search it came from and the test that would confirm it.
misconceptions: Reports a p-value that ignores the search
Exploration is where questions come from; hiding it loses the question
Adds a causal claim and a decision to an untested pattern

questions.prompt: An analyst tries the mean, then the median, then the share above a threshold, and reports the one summary for which two groups differ "significantly". Why is the reported p-value too optimistic?
options: The median is never a valid summary for a test
Three summaries were tried and the best one kept
The groups should have been merged before testing
A threshold always makes a difference look larger
questions.explanation: Each choice made after seeing the result is another comparison. The p-value of the one that was kept ignores the others.
misconceptions: The median is a legitimate summary; the choosing is the issue
Merging the groups would remove the comparison altogether
Not always, and it misses the point about choosing

questions.prompt: A report is rendered twice from the same data and code, and one interval reads 0.41 to 0.58 in the first run and 0.40 to 0.59 in the second. What is the most likely cause and its fix?
options: Resampling without a fixed seed; set the seed as a parameter
Rounding differs between runs; print more decimals
The data changed between runs; lock the file
The two runs used different computers; use one computer
questions.explanation: A bootstrap draws random resamples. Without a fixed seed, each run draws others, and the ends of the interval move.
misconceptions: Rounding is deterministic and gives the same digits each time
The question states that the data was the same
The same seed and versions give the same result on any computer

questions.prompt: A quarterly report reads its headline numbers from a file "summary.csv" that an analyst saved a year ago. Since then, duplicate rows were removed from the raw data. What is the risk?
options: The report will run more slowly than it needs to
The headline numbers no longer follow from the raw data
The summary file may be too large to send by e-mail
The report will show more decimals than the raw data has
questions.explanation: A saved summary keeps the numbers of the day it was saved. Later corrections to the data never reach it.
misconceptions: Speed is the reason caches exist, not their risk
File size is not the issue
Nothing about decimals follows from caching

questions.prompt: A findings table has the columns finding, status, check and limit. Which row is complete and honest?
options: "Discounts cause loyalty" · confirmed · correlation 0.6 · none needed
"Weekend orders are larger" · exploratory · best of 14 cuts · test next quarter
"Sales rose in the north" · confirmed · looked at the chart · none
"Returns fell" · exploratory · no check was run · the data may be wrong
questions.explanation: It names the status truthfully, gives the check with the search behind it, and states what has to happen next.
misconceptions: A causal claim resting on a correlation, with the limit refused
"Confirmed" with no plan, no real check and no limit
No check at all, and a limit too vague to act on

questions.prompt: An exploratory report for a director who is not an analyst is being edited. Which sentence should stay as it is?
options: "The data proves that evening visitors are more satisfied than others."
"In this data, evening visitors rated 0.3 point higher (0.1 to 0.5)."
"Satisfaction is driven by the time of day at which people visit."
"The difference between evening and daytime visitors is significant."
questions.explanation: It says what was seen, in which data and how sure, in words the reader understands, and claims no proof and no cause.
misconceptions: Exploration does not prove
"Driven by" claims a cause that nothing in the data supports
"Significant" with no number means "important" to this reader

questions.prompt: What does it mean for a report to "rerun"?
options: One command rebuilds every number from the raw data
It can be opened again without any software
Its charts can be edited by hand after export
It was reviewed twice before being sent out
questions.explanation: One path leads from the read-only raw data to the page, and anyone can run it and get the same page.
misconceptions: Being readable is not being reproducible
Hand edits break the path from data to page
Review is useful and is a different thing
